11. Iron
Iron is an important nutrient for almost all life. It forms hemoglobin, making it necessary for the transportation
of oxygen in blood. It comprises proteins throughout the body and regulates cell growth and differentiation. It
even helps maintain brain function, metabolism, endocrine function, and immune function and plays a role in
the production of ATP, your body’s primary energy source. But while iron seems to be the darling of many in the
health and medical industries and iron deficiencies are frequently tested for, iron toxicity is rarely addressed.
Because many people are convinced that iron is a panacea, it can be found in everything from multivitamins
to fortified, whole-grain breakfast cereals. Problem is, if you consume too much iron, you can develop iron
overload. Hemochromatosis is a disease characterized by an accumulation of dangerously harmful levels of iron.
This can be an especially concerning issue for men (in women, menstruation helps rid the body of excess iron)
and for sedentary individuals, who don’t turn over as many red blood cells and as much iron as active
individuals, particularly endurance athletes.
As your cells produce energy through normal metabolism, they create low, manageable levels of a toxic by-
product of oxygen called superoxide. Enzymes convert superoxide into hydrogen peroxide, which is then
converted into water and oxygen. But when iron interacts with superoxide or hydrogen peroxide, it leads to a
chemical reaction that produces a free radical known as a hydroxyl radical. Hydroxyl radicals can be extremely
harmful to your cells, and if you are consuming excess iron or have excess iron in your bloodstream, you can
produce high levels of these radicals, leading to age-related chronic conditions such as cancer, heart disease, and
diabetes, and neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Think of this as “rusting” your
body.
Two biomarkers will reveal if you have excess iron. The first is a protein called ferritin. When your iron levels
are sufficient, the protein hepcidin is secreted by the liver and signals the cells in your gastrointestinal tract to
block the absorption of iron. It also signals your body’s other cells to bind their iron to ferritin, which acts as an
iron storage mechanism. If your ferritin levels are high, then you may have too much iron in your body. People
with hereditary hemochromatosis have a genetic inability (based on the HFE gene) to effectively use hepcidin to
regulate iron levels, so they are highly susceptible to iron overload. The typical reference range that most
laboratories use for ferritin is 20 to 300 ng/mL, but the ideal levels for nonmenstruating adults are between 30
and 60 ng/mL, and you don’t want to be below 20 ng/mL or above 80 ng/mL.
If you menstruate, you are more likely to suffer from iron deficiency than iron overload, so if you experience
fatigue, paleness, shortness of breath, headaches, dizziness, heart palpitations, dry or damaged hair and skin,
restless legs, or mouth swelling during your period, you likely need to consume more iron. If you have no
symptoms and your biomarker levels are within the ideal range, then your iron levels are probably being
sufficiently regulated by your menstrual cycle. If you’re a man, you’ll likely only experience issues with low
ferritin or low iron if you’re a heavily training athlete or you’re not eating any red meat.
Another biomarker to track for iron is gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT). GGT is a liver enzyme involved in
the metabolism of the antioxidant glutathione as well as the transport of amino acids and peptides. Originally
tracked to determine the extent of alcoholism and liver damage, GGT is highly interactive with iron and can be
used to track levels of excess free iron (unbound iron in your blood). In fact, GGT has been shown to be the
single most predictive measure of early death by any cause. If you have both high ferritin and high GGT, you
have a significantly increased risk of chronic disease because you have both excess free iron (indicated by GGT)
--- END PAGE 836 ---

--- PAGE 837 ---
and excess stored iron (indicated by ferritin) that keeps those free levels elevated. As with ferritin, the reference
ranges for GGT that are considered “normal” are not the ideal levels. In men, “normal” GGT levels are allowed
to range all the way up to 70 U/L (units per liter), but ideal levels are less than 16 U/L. For women, normal levels
range up to 45 U/L, while ideal levels are less than 9 U/L.
Conveniently, to reduce excess iron levels, all you need to do is give blood two or three times per year,
reduce your intake of red meat, or take up some form of frequent cardiovascular exercise, or all three. Men and
postmenopausal women are particularly at risk for developing iron overload because they don’t lose a significant
amount of blood once a month, so if you fall into one of those categories, then consider giving blood a few times
per year. If you can’t give the liter of blood that’s normally drawn, you can have 2 to 6 ounces of blood drawn
once every few weeks.
12. Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP)
A comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) provides a snapshot of your overall health by measuring various
substances in your blood. It typically includes multiple components that evaluate different organ systems and
metabolic processes. The test is commonly ordered as part of a routine checkup to assess overall health,
diagnose certain medical conditions, monitor ongoing health conditions, or evaluate the effects of medications.
Here are some of the important components typically included in a comprehensive metabolic panel:•

Glucose: Measures the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood. High levels may indicate diabetes or other
metabolic disorders, while low levels may indicate hypoglycemia. As you learned from the discussion of
glycemic variability in chapter 8, I’m a bigger fan of using a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) to track
glucose in real time, but many CMPs include a hemoglobin A1C or HbA1c test, which measures your average
blood sugar levels over the past three months. This can obviously be more insightful than a single snapshot
of blood glucose, although like many reference ranges it must be taken with a grain of salt because HbA1c is
often elevated in those who are anemic and in endurance athletes, because of a shorter-lived time of the red
blood cells. This is a perfect example of knowing when to view lab values in the proper context!
• Incidentally, a Lipoprotein-Insulin Resistance Score (LP-IR) can tell you whether you have signs of insulin
resistance years before hemoglobin A1C or blood glucose shows signs of this problem. Often, LP-IR can be
elevated while HbA1c is normal. An LP-IR is probably the most predictive score of future diabetes risk you
can get, and it only costs around $20 to $50 to include on a lab panel. The LP-IR Score is calculated based on
the levels of specific lipoprotein subclasses, including very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), low-density
lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles, along with their respective sizes. This score
is presented on a scale (such as 0 to 100), with a higher score indicating a greater degree of insulin
resistance.•

Electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride): These minerals help maintain the balance of fluids in the body
and are crucial for nerve and muscle function. Abnormal levels can indicate dehydration, kidney problems, or
hormonal imbalances. Chloride is an example of lab value that can advise you on specific dietary or lifestyle
factors, because high chloride can indicate that you have metabolic acidosis (having too much acid in your
blood, or a lower-than-normal blood pH, often due to high intake of acidic foods or low intake of minerals)
or respiratory alkalosis, which is a low level of carbon dioxide in your blood due to shallow breathing,
excessive breathing, or hyperventilating.•

Calcium: Important for bone health, muscle function, and nerve transmission. High or low levels can
indicate issues with the parathyroid gland, kidneys, or bones.
--- END PAGE 837 ---

--- PAGE 838 ---
•

Kidney function tests (blood urea nitrogen [BUN], creatinine): These tests evaluate how well the kidneys
are functioning by measuring waste products in the blood. Abnormal levels can indicate kidney disease or
other kidney-related issues, although elevated creatinine and BUN can also simply mean you’re
supplementing with creatine or you did a hard workout in the one to two days prior to the test.•

Liver function tests (albumin, total protein, alkaline phosphatase, alanine aminotransferase [ALT],
aspartate aminotransferase [AST], bilirubin): These tests assess the health of the liver and its ability to
metabolize substances. Abnormal levels can indicate liver disease, hepatitis, or other liver disorders and can
often give you insight about whether you might be drinking too much alcohol or using too many herbs,
supplements, or pharmaceuticals that stress the liver—a common problem among biohackers and health
enthusiasts.•

Total protein and albumin: Measures the total amounts of protein and albumin in the blood, which can
indicate liver or kidney disease, malnutrition, or other conditions, including excessive protein intake or poor
protein breakdown.• 
Bilirubin: Measures the levels of a waste product produced by the breakdown of red blood cells. Abnormal
levels can indicate liver or bile duct problems, excess red blood cell turnover from high amounts of
endurance exercise, or, once again, that you simply worked out too hard in the days leading up to your test.
Overall, a CMP is a valuable tool for assessing overall health, diagnosing medical conditions, monitoring
ongoing health conditions, and guiding decisions about lifestyle, exercise, and diet modifications. However, it’s
important to interpret the results in conjunction with other clinical information and consult with a healthcare
professional for proper diagnosis and management.
13. Vitamin D
Vitamin D is quite possibly the most important vitamin to pay attention to on a lab test since it is a crucial
nutrient that plays a fundamental role in a host of physiological processes. While it’s commonly associated with
bone health and calcium absorption, emerging research has highlighted vitamin D’s diverse functions in
supporting immune function, cardiovascular health, mood regulation, resistance to infection, and overall well-
being. Low levels of vitamin D have been linked to a myriad of health concerns, including increased
susceptibility to infections, autoimmune diseases, cardiovascular disease, cognitive decline, and mood disorders.
But, like many lab results, more vitamin D is not better, and excess vitamin D levels often indicate risk for
vascular calcification (VC). Calcification occurs when calcium deposits accumulate in soft tissues, such as
arteries, heart valves, and kidneys, leading to arterial stiffness, cardiovascular disease, and kidney stones.
Excessive vitamin D intake, either through supplementation or sun exposure, can lead to hypercalcemia, a
condition characterized by elevated levels of calcium in the blood. Hypercalcemia can result in symptoms such
as nausea, vomiting, weakness, confusion, and even organ damage if left untreated. Prolonged hypercalcemia can
contribute to the formation of calcifications in various tissues, increasing the risk of cardiovascular events and
kidney dysfunction, particularly if vitamin D is elevated in the absence of adequate vitamin K and magnesium
intake.
The optimal range for vitamin D levels is between 40 and 80 ng/mL. Levels below 20 ng/mL are indicative of
vitamin D deficiency, while levels above 80 ng/mL may increase the risk of adverse effects, including
calcification.
There are other subtle nuances to pay attention to when testing vitamin D. For example, in the presence of
excess lead exposure from paint, pipes, contaminated soil, children’s toys and jewelry, drinking water, or other
environmental sources, your body forcefully lowers vitamin D as a protective mechanism. Obviously, if you don’t
--- END PAGE 838 ---

--- PAGE 839 ---
test your lead levels via a hair or blood analysis, you wouldn’t know that your vitamin D is low not because you
aren’t taking enough, but rather due to lead exposure. Vitamin D is also a negative acute phase reactant, meaning
that concentrations decrease during inflammation. So inflammation, not a lack of vitamin D supplementation or
inadequate sun exposure, could also be a reason vitamin D is too low, and a blood test could be an unreliable
biomarker of vitamin D levels if you have had an acute inflammatory insult such as an injury or you suffer
chronic inflammation from stress, lack of sleep, or other environmental factors. Finally, glutathione plays a key
role in vitamin D metabolism, and often a glutathione deficiency can contribute to low vitamin D levels.
Glutathione intake alone can increase vitamin D in the absence of additional vitamin D supplementation! As you
can see, similar to other lab results, when it comes to vitamin D, everything needs to be taken in the proper
context.
14. Apolipoprotein B (ApoB)
When it comes to lipids, the terms “good” cholesterol and “bad” cholesterol are a bit antiquated, because both
LDL and HDL serve important functions. Similarly, the idea that diet is the main factor that impacts blood
cholesterol levels is also antiquated. Fact is, about 80 percent of the circulating cholesterol in your body is
produced by your cells, not consumed through your diet. This means dietary cholesterol is very unlikely to be
the major driver of cholesterol levels in your bloodstream since most of your blood cholesterol comes from your
body creating its own cholesterol, not from all those eggs you’re eating or not eating.
This is why it’s important to pay attention to specific components of lipoproteins, which are the shuttles that
carry cholesterol around and across tissues and organs. ApoB is a protein that wraps around these lipoproteins,
including low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL). It serves as a structural
component of these lipoproteins, facilitating the transport of cholesterol and other fats throughout the body.
Higher levels of ApoB suggest you have more particles in your blood that may trigger a cascade of heart attack or
stroke, and elevated ApoB levels have been shown to be associated with an increased risk of atherosclerosis and
cardiovascular events. Calcium buildup in the arteries is now understood to be related to the number of ApoB
lipoprotein B carriers. This makes it pretty surprising that ApoB testing is not a part of the standard lipid profile
your physician may order.
Ideal levels of ApoB are 90 nmol/L or less. When I discovered that I had significant plaque accumulation and
ApoB levels above 170, I experimented with a variety of strategies to lower ApoB, and eventually—after trying
natural solutions such as niacin, red yeast rice extract, nattokinase, and vitamin K—found near-immediate
success with a three-month stint of a twice-monthly injection of a PCSK9 inhibitor, which increases LDL
receptors in the liver, decreases LDL cholesterol levels in the blood, and has been shown to be a good way to
lower ApoB. With this strategy, I was able to plummet my ApoB down to below 70.
15. Lipoprotein A [Lp(a)]
Lp(a) is a type of lipoprotein particle similar to low-density lipoprotein (LDL), but it contains an additional
protein called apolipoprotein(a) attached to the LDL particle. Lp(a) is a known risk factor for cardiovascular
disease and is implicated in the development of atherosclerosis. Elevated levels of Lp(a) in the blood are
associated with an increased risk of heart attack, stroke, and other cardiovascular events, even independent of
traditional risk factors such as high LDL cholesterol levels, and are five to ten times more predictive of
cardiovascular events than other lipid measurements!
An optimal range for Lp(a) is less than 14 mg/dL. It’s important to know that, similar to how you can have a
normal lipid panel but an elevated plaque score in the heart, you can have a normal ApoB on a lab test and
--- END PAGE 839 ---

--- PAGE 840 ---
normal cholesterol on a standard lipid panel but still have high Lp(a). This is important because high Lp(a) is
about twenty-five times more likely to cause a heart attack than high LDL! Once again, considering that the
Lp(a) and ApoB tests cost about $10 each, I find it a bit shocking that these tests are not standard measurements
a doctor orders on a regularly scheduled lipid panel to check up on heart health.
The Bottom Line
So there you have it. Sure, you should certainly pay attention to variables such as love, stress, relationships, diet,
fasting, grip strength, and more. But you should also track the important biomarkers listed here, which can give
you early warnings about accelerated aging and increased risk of mortality. Because so many of these biomarkers
are not included on a standard blood panel, you’ll need to either order these tests for yourself from one of the
services included on the resources page for this chapter or ask your doctor for them.
HOW TO TEST YOUR HORMONES
Because hormone levels fluctuate throughout the day, the gold-standard method for testing your hormones is
the DUTCH urine steroid hormone profile, which is performed via multiple collections throughout the day—all
in the comfort of your home. It is a good way to see what’s truly going on with your hormones because it doesn’t
measure just hormones but also hormone metabolites. Since steroid hormones do not dissolve well in water,
they cannot pass directly into the urine and instead must be broken down in the liver and kidneys to form
smaller water-soluble particles known as metabolites. These metabolites can be extremely important indicators
for certain conditions and give an in-depth picture of why hormones are elevated, lacking, or point toward
specific symptoms.
Measuring both hormones and their metabolites can give you or your healthcare practitioner a much better
overall picture of hormone production. For example, someone whose salivary test shows low cortisol could
discover through a DUTCH urine steroid hormone profile that they have normal cortisol production but high
levels of metabolites—in other words, they produce enough cortisol, but it’s getting broken down very quickly,
or vice versa, which can indicate hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, long-term stress, inflammation, insulin
resistance, infection, poor liver function, anorexia, critical illness, and more.
With serum (blood) and saliva hormone spot-testing, it’s possible to track variations in hormone release
throughout the day—and this is a great way to measure how your hormones change during a twenty-four-hour
period. In contrast, a standard twenty-four-hour urine collection many physicians use reflects your total
hormone output in a twenty-four-hour period. But by using the DUTCH urine steroid test, you get the best of all
worlds: blood, saliva, and urinary results with just a urine collection. The DUTCH test measures the following:
• Free cortisone (a corticosteroid related to cortisol)
• Creatinine (a by-product of creatine breakdown)
• Free cortisol. Most circulating cortisol is bound to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin; less than 5
percent is unbound. Only free cortisol can reach the enzyme transporters in the kidneys, liver, and other
organs involved in excretory and metabolic clearance.
• Tetrahydrocortisone, a-tetrahydrocortisol, and b-tetrahydrocortisol (all metabolites of cortisol breakdown)
• DHEA (a precursor for estrogens and testosterone; see here)
• The progesterone metabolites a-pregnanediol and b-pregnanediol
--- END PAGE 840 ---

--- PAGE 841 ---
• The androgen metabolites etiocholanolone, androsterone, testosterone, 5a-DHT, 5a-androstanediol, 5b-
androstanediol, and epi-testosterone
• The estrogen metabolites estrone, estradiol, estriol, 2-OH-estrone, 4-OH-estrone, 16-OH-estrone, 2-
methoxyestrone, and 2-OH-estradiol
• 6-OH-melatonin-sulfate (the major active metabolite of melatonin)
Testing with DUTCH is easy. When you order a test, a collection kit is sent straight to your door, and the kit
includes five easy-to-use filter paper devices on which you urinate. You then use the enclosed prepaid label to
send them back to the lab. Your DUTCH results include helpful, actionable tips for adjusting hormones using
diet, lifestyle, and supplementation strategies.
HOW TO TEST FOR FOOD SENSITIVITIES
I prefer to use Cyrex Labs for food-sensitivity testing because their tests are highly accurate, consistent, and
based on the latest research and development in food-sensitivity analysis. Unlike outdated tests that test only
one form of a given food, Cyrex tests multiple forms (raw, cooked, and processed) and food cross-reactions and
identifies only foods that challenge your immune system so you can reduce the load on your immune system by
minimizing exposure to those foods.
I particularly like Cyrex because it produces fewer false positives than other food-sensitivity tests. It’s quite
popular these days for health enthusiasts to order tests advertised as ALCAT tests (you can even buy them on
Amazon!). Many of these tests use an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), which tests allergies and
sensitivities to a variety of common allergens, or an antibody assessment panel that tests for IgG and IgA. I had
this panel done on myself and discovered that I can’t tolerate dairy from cows (but not from goats) and chicken
eggs (but not eggs from other fowl, such as ducks).
Considering the amount of omelets, raw-dairy yogurt and cheese, Greek yogurt, and protein bars containing
whey from grass-fed cows that I was consuming at the time, it was impossible to ascertain which came first, the
food sensitivities or the high levels of antibodies circulating in my bloodstream because I was eating those foods.
And herein lies the problem with blood-based food-intolerance testing: the presence of antibodies to certain
foods does not necessarily mean that those foods are causing a harmful immune reaction. It more likely means
that those are the foods you eat the most often or have eaten the most recently.
In fact, people who were allergic to milk or eggs as kids but eventually outgrew those allergies (which is fairly
common) tend to have more antibodies to those foods. In other words, the presence of antibodies is linked to an
increased tolerance for those foods, not a decreased tolerance. Yet when you test yourself, you may receive a long
and foreboding list of foods to avoid (often hundreds of them!) when they may not be your problem.
This is why, for the best accuracy, I recommend the Array 3, Array 4, and Array 10 tests from Cyrex Labs,
which will give you plenty of information without producing false positives or giving you a frustrating, extremely
long list of foods that you can’t eat. This is due to many reasons, including these:
• Food that’s been heated above 118 degrees Fahrenheit experiences changes in its protein structure and thus
its antigenicity. Cyrex screens for raw and cooked forms of common foods on their Array 10.
• Some antigens are cross-reactive, meaning that antibodies developed for one food also respond to another
food. Cyrex tests for reactivity to these cross-reactive antigens, as well as for reactivity to pan-antigens like
parvalbumin and latex hevein.
• Instead of testing only for reactivity to individual proteins, Cyrex also tests for reactivity to food
combinations.
--- END PAGE 841 ---

--- PAGE 842 ---
• Many food products, especially gluten-free foods, substitute gums for gluten to hold the food together. Cyrex
tests for sensitivity to these gums.
• Binding isolates like lectins and agglutinins tend to affect specific tissues. Cyrex tests for sensitivity to these
isolates.
• Cyrex measures your reactivity to artificial food colorings.
• Oils that were once thought to be uncontaminated by proteins actually contain hidden proteins called
oleosins. Cyrex tests for reactivity to oleosins.
• Meat glue is used to hold meat together (it’s crazy what food manufacturers do these days, huh?). So, in
addition to testing for reactivity to meat, Cyrex also tests for reactivity to meat glue.
• Some people produce more IgA or more IgG. Cyrex combines the two into one panel to reduce the chance of
missing reactivity.
On your results, Cyrex gives three ranges of results: “normal,” “equivocal,” and “out of range.” “Normal”
indicates an immune response within the accepted range, “equivocal” is one standard deviation away from a
normal result, and “out of range” is two points of deviation from normal.
You should consider any “out of range” result to mean that the food is provoking a serious immune response.
An “equivocal” result is also significant and may mean you are just beginning to exhibit an immune reaction to a
food, and temporary elimination of that food—as well as addressing issues such as a leaky gut or implementing
other strategies from chapter 13—is a very good idea. If you test positive for immune sensitivity to many foods,
remove only the ones you react to the most (the “out of range” scores) and begin a protocol to restore tolerance.
After several weeks, you can test again, and if fewer foods come back positive, it’s a sign you are on the right
track.
The Cyrex Array 10, also called the Multiple Food Immune Reactivity Screen, measures reactivity to 180 food
antigens, including reactions to foods in cooked, raw, and/or modified forms. This can help you customize which
foods to eat and avoid. Of all the Cyrex panels, I consider the Array 10 to give you the best bang for your buck
when it comes to food-sensitivity testing. Other useful Cyrex panels include the Array 4 (gluten-associated
cross-reactivity), Array 11 (chemical immune reactivity), and Array 10C, which combines all their best food-
allergy tests into one highly informative panel that evaluates over 180 different food antigens and cross-
reactivities. A newer test that is similar to the Cyrex tests but can be even more sensitive for wheat- or gluten-
related issues is the Gut Zoomer, a blood sample test that can also give precise results about foods causing
sensitivities and intolerances.
Another way to test for food allergies is via a microbiome panel, which can give clues about food allergy or
intolerance risks based on gut flora. More details on this type of testing are in chapter 13. Research has shown
that people with food allergies experience differences in their gut flora, which, in turn, suggests that changes in
your gut microbiome impact the development of allergies and intolerances. A normal human microbiome
includes a wide range of bacteria, including enterobacteriaceae, bacteroides, lactobacilli, and bifidobacteria, and
reduced numbers of these microbes has been shown to impair the immune system, leading to allergies or
intolerances.
For example, reduced levels of lactobacilli and increased levels of Staphylococcus aureus are correlated with
milk and egg allergies. Reduced numbers of L. casei, L. paracasei, L. rhamnosus, and Bifidobacterium adolescentis
have been associated with egg white allergies and allergies to cow’s milk. Lower levels of actinobacteria,
proteobacteria, and bacteroides have also been correlated with general allergies and intolerances. Research has
also suggested that if you have poor gut flora diversity, you may be predisposed to intolerance of gluten,
FODMAPs, and histamines. When it comes to gluten in particular, certain bacterial strains can aid your digestive
system in breaking down gluten proteins, which means that if you lack these strains, you’re more likely to have a
--- END PAGE 842 ---

--- PAGE 843 ---
gluten intolerance. SIBO (small intestine bacterial overgrowth) is known to result in FODMAP intolerances and
is caused by a lack of beneficial gut bacteria. Similarly, an overgrowth of histamine- or enzyme-producing
bacteria that interferes with histamine metabolism can result in histamine intolerances.
Finally, many symptoms of food allergies or intolerances are actually brought on by mold and mycotoxin
exposure. Using the types of toxin tests you’ll find on the online resources page for this chapter, you can
measure levels of c4a, TGF-beta-1, MSH, VIP, VEGF, MMP-9, and leptins, which give a snapshot of how the
immune system may have been impacted by mold toxicity. Markedly elevated levels of c4a, TGF-beta-1, MMP-9,
and leptins and low levels of MSH, VIP, and VEGF all point in that direction. You can find a physician well versed
in this type of testing on the website SurvivingMold.com, and chapters 4 and 20 address in detail how to manage
mold and mycotoxin exposure.
HOW TO TEST FOR MICRONUTRIENT DEFICIENCIES
Sometimes you need to take a deep dive into smaller variables that a basic blood test doesn’t look into, such as
amino acids, fatty acids, antioxidants, minerals, metabolites, enzymes, inflammatory markers, and more. For this
purpose, you can use an at-home test like the Metabolomix+ from Genova Diagnostics, which is a unique
combination of nutritional tests that provides an analysis of key nutritional biomarkers. A first morning void
(FMV) urine collection, with an optional add-on bloodspot finger stick and buccal swab, the Metabolomix+ test
is a noninvasive way to assess the functional need for antioxidants, B-vitamins, minerals, digestive support, fatty
acids, and amino acids. It also tests for a variety of nutrient, detoxification, and cell regulation markers, as well
as bacterial and yeast/fungal compounds.
Over time, deficiencies in these compounds can cause a variety of chronic health conditions, and if you
struggle with things like poor sleep, less-than-stellar workouts, brain fog, appetite cravings, sore joints, or other
“mysterious” issues, this profile can help elucidate deficiencies in micronutrients and other small components
that other basic blood tests simply can’t discover. The results from a Metabolomix+ test include a suggested
supplement schedule that offers personalized recommendations and a helpful at-a-glance interpretation page
that provides facts on nutrient function, causes and complications of their deficiencies, and dietary sources.
A more affordable and convenient way to test for micronutrients and minerals is a hair tissue mineral
analysis (HTMA). This diagnostic tool assesses mineral levels and heavy metal toxicity in the body by analyzing a
small sample of hair (I don’t like to mess up my precisely engineered haircut, so I just take a small snip of hair
from my crotch, which is perfectly acceptable for accurate results). This noninvasive test provides valuable
insight into the body’s mineral status and potential imbalances, offering a comprehensive overview of overall
health and potential nutritional deficiencies or toxic exposures. The lab analysis examines the concentrations of
various minerals and heavy metals present in your hair, reflecting your body’s mineral metabolism and potential
exposure to environmental toxins over time.
When I took my first HTMA interpretation course from Dr. Leland Stillman, I realized that for only a
hundred bucks, an HTMA offers an impressive array of insights into health and well-being. First, it provides
information about mineral deficiencies or excesses that may impact various physiological processes. For
example, imbalances in or improper ratios of essential minerals like calcium, magnesium, zinc, and potassium
can affect energy production, hormone regulation, immune function, and nerve transmission. Identifying these
imbalances via HTMA allows for targeted nutritional interventions to restore or balance mineral levels.
Additionally, HTMA can detect toxic exposure to heavy metals, such as lead, mercury, cadmium, and arsenic,
which can accumulate in the body over time and contribute to chronic health issues.
--- END PAGE 843 ---

--- PAGE 844 ---
These types of imbalances, deficiencies, or excesses can serve as clues to do further, more advanced blood,
stool, saliva, or urinary analysis. For example, let’s say you’ve been experiencing blood sugar issues, and your
HTMA shows a chromium deficiency. Chromium is involved in glucose metabolism and blood sugar regulation,
and abnormal chromium levels can impact insulin function and contribute to blood sugar imbalances,
potentially leading to diabetes or other metabolic disorders. Or let’s say your vitamin D is chronically low, no
matter how much you supplement or how much sunshine you get. Your HTMA may show a high load of metals
such as lead or abnormal levels of antioxidants such as manganese and copper, both issues that can lower
vitamin D levels. An experienced practitioner can quickly identify issues like these on an HTMA, and you can
learn quite a bit from taking an HTMA interpretation course such as the one I took from Dr. Stillman. I’ll include
a link to that course on the online resources page for this chapter.
HOW TO TEST YOUR GUT
There are approximately 40 trillion microorganisms living in your gut, where they make up your gut microbiome.
They help digest your food, produce beneficial and harmful chemicals, control infections from pathogens,
regulate your immune system, and even control your emotions (ever have a “gut feeling”?). Some of these
microorganisms have been implicated in maintaining optimal health, while others can contribute to many
chronic conditions, including diabetes, obesity, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, coronary artery disease, psoriasis,
lupus, and autism. By taking care of your 40 trillion microbe friends, you can maximize your wellness and
potentially prevent disease.
In chapter 13, I told you most of what you need to know about testing your microbiome. As you learned in
that chapter, if you suspect that you have insufficient gut bacteria levels or want to adjust your diet and
supplementation routine for your unique gut profile, I recommend a one-two combo: the three-day Genova gut-
testing kit to test for the presence of bacteria, which uses short sequences called primers to look for specific
microbes using a PCR analysis, along with a microbiome analysis, which is offered by companies such as Viome,
Wellnicity, BIOHM, Psomagen, Ombre, and Thorne and uses metagenomics to assess bacterial abundance and
overall microbial function and screen for stealth gut infections. These types of microbiome tests can even
identify the metabolites produced by the microbes in your gut and provide personalized diet and lifestyle
recommendations to fine-tune the function of your gut microbiome to minimize the production of harmful
metabolites and maximize the production of beneficial ones.
HOW TO TEST YOUR GENES
I’ve been testing and tracking my genetics for over ten years—not because it’s necessary to constantly retest
your genetics (unless you’re engaged in some kind of regularly scheduled, aggressive gene-editing experiments)
but because I find it informative and interesting to see what kind of data one can get from a few simple drops of
saliva or blood. After all, if you know where your ancestors came from, what they ate, and what diseases or
predispositions you might have floating around in your body, you’ll be far better equipped to make targeted diet,
supplementation, exercise, and lifestyle modifications.
For the most part, all DNA tests are quite similar: First, you provide some personal background information,
and then you order a test kit. After that, you provide your DNA sample via a finger-prick blood sample, saliva
deposit, or cheek swab. You then mail it to the lab and wait for your results. However, there are some variations
depending on the type of test you use and your reason for taking a DNA test. Different labs employ different
--- END PAGE 844 ---

--- PAGE 845 ---
methods to analyze DNA samples based on the focus of the results, and some tests only assess specific sections
of the DNA, while others analyze the entire genome.
DNA tests use various techniques, including DNA methylation, to make predictions about your health state.
Tests that also check for ancestry often use a technique called genotyping to gather results. This process involves
studying an individual’s DNA sequence to determine variants in their genetic makeup that are unique to them.
Another method called autosomal DNA testing measures autosomal chromosomes and matches them across a
database to connect individuals to unknown relatives.
This type of self-quantification is important because genes can reveal information about your predisposition
to certain diseases, your overall nutritional health, and any vitamin or mineral deficiencies you may be at risk of
developing. While your genetic code cannot be altered to reduce your susceptibility to a given disease (at least,
not yet with great precision or safety), DNA tests can provide meaningful insight into how your body functions,
which allows you to take proactive measures to reduce your likelihood of developing a certain disease. For
instance, if a test identifies a gene linked to heart disease, you can prioritize early preventative actions you may
not have otherwise taken, such as a robust sauna practice, mineral intake, exercise that is adequate but not too
hard, and meditation or other stress-control tactics.
The accuracy and precision of DNA health test kits largely depend on various factors, including the sample
type, the method of analysis, the database size, the algorithm used to produce results, the amount of DNA
studied (specific sections versus the entire sequence), and the reproducibility (result consistency under
different conditions). With advancements in science and technology, at-home genetic testing kits have become
increasingly accurate in providing key health insights.
Perhaps the most popular DNA test is 23andMe, which offers an ancestry service that helps you understand
who you are, where your DNA comes from, and your family story. 23andMe analyzes, compiles, and distills your
DNA information into helpful reports about your ancestry and provides a tool to enable you to connect with
relatives who share similar DNA, along with providing insights on your health predispositions and risks, such as
how fast you metabolize caffeine or your likelihood for having migraines. AncestryDNA’s service is similar but a
bit more focused on deep historical research to build out a family tree. Their database contains more than 18
million profiles, making it the largest of all the DNA test kit services. They also maintain a powerful tool for
searching through hundreds of historical document databases.
If you’re a workout junkie, DNAfit is a good service to upload your genetic data to, especially if you’re active
and want to know more about how to exercise and eat. DNAfit can determine your response to a selection of key
genetic markers associated with health, fitness, nutrition, and athletic performance, and it provides an in-depth
analysis of up to forty-five key genetic variants, allowing you to tailor your training and nutrition choices to play
to your genetic advantage. The DNAfit Nutrigenetic report uses DNA data to provide information about your
response to carbohydrate and fats; detoxification (phase 1 and phase 2) ability; antioxidant capacity; omega-3
and vitamins B and D needs; salt, alcohol, and caffeine sensitivity; lactose intolerance; and celiac disease
predisposition. The DNAfit Fitness report uses DNA information to provide information regarding your
response to power training versus endurance genetics, aerobic (VO max) response, recovery profile, and injury
2 risk.
Companies like 10X, The DNA Company, StrateGene, 3X4 Genetics, and SelfDecode operate at the forefront
of personalized health by leveraging advanced genomic science to provide a comprehensive understanding of
your genetic makeup. Unlike traditional DNA testing services that often focus on ancestry or limited health
markers, these services go several steps further by offering a 360-degree view of your genetic blueprint,
interpreting how genetic variants interact and influence overall health. StrateGene, designed by my friend and
former podcast guest Dr. Ben Lynch, dives into specific “dirty” genes that you should pay the most attention to,
such as folate, methionine, sulfur, glutathione, and histamine pathways, providing advice about compounds and
lifestyle activities that speed up or slow down each gene. For education on your genetics, SelfDecode offers one
--- END PAGE 845 ---

--- PAGE 846 ---
of the most comprehensive genetic models on the market. For example, their report on blood pressure looks at
nearly a million genetic variants (SNPs)! For comparison, 23andMe’s blood pressure report looks at only 3,000
SNPs. SelfDecode then designs reports built on AI and machine learning technology. By using a technique called
genetic imputation, their system turns the roughly 500,000 SNPs that most genotyping chips cover into data for
over 83 million additional variants, all with an accuracy rate of 99.7 percent. This enables SelfDecode to analyze
up to seventy times more of your genome than other companies can, which massively improves the accuracy of
your genetic results and personalized health recommendations.
Should you want to take the deepest dive into your DNA, you can get whole genome sequencing (WGS),
which gives you a complete blueprint of your entire DNA. When you receive your results, you will have
information on more than three billion genetic variants, or changes in your genome. Even genes whose purpose
are not yet known are included. This means that years in the future, your sequencing results will still be relevant
and applicable to the latest genetic findings. This testing is not as expensive as you’d think: the cost of a whole
genome sequence decreased from an estimated $1 million in 2007 to $1,000 in 2014, and today it costs about
$600. Companies that offer WGS include Gencove, Dante Labs, 23andMe, Illumina, and Nebula.
Finally, many biological age measurements use the science of epigenetics to determine the age of your body,
organs, and cells and your potential to function for years ahead. This biological age is often different from
chronological age, and many are surprised to find they’re aging faster than they think. For each year that you’re
biologically older than your chronological age, your statistical probability for disease and death increases, but
fortunately, the opposite is also true: for each year you’re biologically younger, your risk decreases.
There are a variety of biological age measurements available, including the epigenetic clock, which is a
biochemical assessment that analyzes DNA; extrinsic immune age, which measures epigenetic changes in
immune cells and how they relate to immunosenescence; telomere tests, which measure the rate at which
telomeres become shorter as DNA is damaged; a PhenoAge or GlycanAge test, which measures common age-
related biomarkers that change during aging; and a DunedinPACE test (described in chapter 9), which measures
the pace of biological aging by analyzing methylation patterns. You don’t have to go to a fancy clinic to get a test
like this; companies like Novos, TruAge, Elysium, GlycanAge, and myDNAge now ship kits directly to your home.
--- END PAGE 846 ---

--- PAGE 847 ---
Should You Train Based on Your Genetics?
You’ve seen it before: there’s that person at the gym who has been training only half as long and half as hard as you
and seems to be making twice the gains and getting twice the results. They must be on steroids, right? Not
necessarily. It’s possible that they’re simply performing the exact number of sets and reps and using the precise
weights that are appropriate for their genetics, while you’re possibly training with a strategy that flies completely in
the face of your own genetics.
While sports scientists have long suspected that elite athletes are born and not necessarily formed in the gym, a
growing body of research studies are now revealing literally dozens of genetic variants that are linked to highly
individualized training responses and sport-related traits. Elite sports coaches from countries such as Russia and China
are now taking this to the next level by selecting the right candidates for the right sports and then personalizing each
athlete’s training based on their unique genetic profiles.
One recent study from Europe impressively demonstrated that matching your genotype with the appropriate training
modality can lead to a far more effective resistance training protocol. The researchers set out to develop an algorithm
that would allow athletes to achieve greater results in response to high- or low-intensity resistance training programs
by predicting each athlete’s potential based on the power and endurance qualities of their genetics using fifteen
performance-associated gene polymorphisms.
In the study, athletes completed an eight-week high- or low-intensity resistance training program that was either
matched or mismatched with their individual genotype (based on information such as whether they appeared to be
genetically equipped with slow-twitch or fast-twitch muscle, levels of mitochondrial density, repair and recovery
mechanisms, and antioxidant production). They were given pre- and post-training performance tests for both
explosive power and endurance capacity. The study was double-blind, and both researchers and athletes were
unaware of the “genetic potential status” of each individual athlete, which was determined by an algorithm developed
by DNAfit.
--- END PAGE 847 ---

--- PAGE 848 ---
The results were astounding. Training according to your genes produced impressive results. Those with the power
genotype who trained with high-intensity, low-rep training and those with the endurance genotype who trained with
low-intensity, high-rep training had performance gains up to 610 percent greater than the participants who trained
with the opposite training protocol from what their genetics dictated! Nearly 82 percent of the low or non-responders
in the study were from the genetically mismatched groups who were training using the wrong training program for
their genetics.
The researchers summarized that “matching the individual’s genotype with the appropriate training modality leads to
more effective resistance training” and that “the developed algorithm may be used to guide individualized resistance-
training interventions.” The big takeaway is this: if you do indeed get a DNAfit test that tells you how you should be
training based on your endurance or power responder profile, you’d most likely benefit big-time from paying attention
to those recommendations! For example, I am nearly 90 percent on the power responder scale, and my body fares far
better for both performance and recovery when I train with heavy weights in an explosive manner as opposed to light
weight with high reps, whereas my friend and endurance responder Kelly Starrett noticed huge performance
breakthroughs when he adopted the opposite approach.
HOW TO TEST BLOOD GLUCOSE AND KETONES
Knowing how your body is responding to its fuel can be key to understanding why you’re having trouble losing
weight, why you’re crashing during a workout, or whether your diet is correctly keyed in to your individual
needs. That’s where blood glucose monitors and ketone meters come in.
Testing Your Blood Glucose
While a single blood test using an inexpensive blood glucose monitor from any drugstore or health website can
give you a static snapshot of your blood glucose levels, nothing beats a continuous blood glucose monitor for
truly determining how your diet is affecting one of the most important parameters of your health and fitness:
glycemic variability.
--- END PAGE 848 ---

--- PAGE 849 ---
A continuous glucose monitoring system (CGM) is just what it sounds like: a system that monitors your
blood sugar continuously, twenty-four hours a day. A sensor is inserted right beneath your skin and attaches to a
transmitter that sends the data to the receiver. You are then able to see your blood sugar level at any point with
the receiver or a phone app.
The sensor is usually inserted with a simple at-home device under the skin of your abdomen or on the back
or your arm and is typically worn for seven to fourteen days. (In my opinion, if you are eating your normal diet
and you eat the same things regularly, you’ll know everything you need to know about your blood glucose after
two weeks and can stop testing at that point, unless you’re wearing the CGM for medical reasons.) If your diet
widely varies or you’re simply a supremely curious self-quantifier, you can of course wear a CGM continuously.
This sensor reads glucose levels in the interstitial fluid below your skin’s surface, and the transmitter it’s linked
to sends this information wirelessly to a receiver or smartphone app (or an insulin pump, if you’re diabetic and
using one). This means that at any given time during the day or night, you can look at your phone or receiver and
see how your blood glucose level is trending, and you can even receive instant notifications if it gets too high or
too low.
In CGM studies of healthy people, a normal fasting blood sugar is approximately 83 mg/dL or less, and in
very metabolically healthy, active individuals, it’s in the mid to high 70s. Unfortunately, most doctors accept
anything under 100 mg/dL as normal, but studies have shown that people with fasting blood sugar levels above
95 have more than three times the risk of developing diabetes than people with levels below 90.
Even more important than fasting blood glucose is the amount of time your blood sugar is elevated over the
level known to increase disease risk, which is about 140 mg/dL. Ideally, after a meal—even a high-carb one—
blood sugar should rise to around 120–130 mg/dL for about forty-five minutes and then drop, reaching less than
100 mg/dL by the two-hour mark.
One caveat is that if you are eating a very-low-carb or ketogenic diet, you may see elevated fasting blood
glucose levels. This is because low-carb diets cause a natural drop in insulin levels and some amount of insulin
resistance. When carbohydrates are restricted, fatty acids are freed up for use as a fuel, which means that in the
long term, muscles have less need for sugar and thus become less sensitive to insulin. So, if you eat a low-carb or
ketogenic diet and have a somewhat high fasting blood sugar (e.g., above 90–100), this is not important, and you
should instead pay closer attention to your postprandial blood sugar levels.
The two most popular CGMs—both of which I’ve experimented with and found to work well, especially
when covered in kinesiotape or some kind of elastic bandage for high-intensity workouts, races, swimming, or
sauna exposure—are the Dexcom and the FreeStyle Libre. Admittedly, I was nervous about using a continuous
blood glucose monitor because I worried that with my active lifestyle, it would constantly become detached
from my body, it would become water-damaged, or the tiny sensor needle would become bent. But as long as I
am careful to tape the CGM prior to intense physical activity, it seems to stay attached well and continues to
take good readings (this is especially true for the more expensive but far more accurate Dexcom G6 model). The
Simpatch adhesive patch for Dexcom works particularly well, as does a strip of properly cut kinesiotape.
Newer, noninvasive CGM technology being developed includes the optical rotation method, which uses a
visible light source to measure glucose levels in the cornea and aqueous humor of the eye; microwave sensors,
which measure blood sugar levels by using the reflection and absorption of microwave signals when they pass
through human tissues; and electromagnetic sensor systems that function much like a small, wearable MRI.
Wearables are increasingly implementing CGM data also, with rings and straps like Ultrahuman, Noise, and
Biosensor pulling your glucose data into the same platform as your stress, sleep, and activity data.
Testing Your Ketones
--- END PAGE 849 ---

--- PAGE 850 ---
In addition to blood glucose, ketone levels can offer good insight into your body. Ketones, you’ll recall from
chapter 4, are produced during fatty acid breakdown, and your ketone levels reflect how efficiently you are
burning fat or producing energy, even in the absence of high blood glucose levels. Assuming you do not possess
genes that would make you respond deleteriously to a high-fat, low-carb diet (as explained in chapter 13), ketosis
can be a powerful nutritional approach to switching your metabolism to prioritizing fat as a fuel while also
increasing cognitive and physical performance. (Incidentally, even if you’re not achieving ketosis via a high-fat,
low-carb diet, you can still amp up ketone production with intermittent fasting or another form of calorie or
carbohydrate restriction.) Many people assume that if they are eating low-carb or fasting, they are in ketosis, but
actually measuring ketones can be useful, especially if you’re just getting used to a new diet or supplement and
are trying to determine whether it increases ketone production. Ideal blood levels of ketones to indicate that you
are in a state of ketosis range from at least 0.5 millimolar up to 3.0 millimolar.
There are three testing methods for ketosis because there are three forms of ketones in your body:
acetoacetate, which can be tested in your urine; acetate, which can be tested in your breath; and beta-
hydroxybutyrate, which can be tested in your blood.
Let’s begin with acetoacetate. The way ketones get into your urine is if they are “spilling over” in excessive
amounts. This means that if there is an excess of ketones, or if you are not utilizing ketones efficiently, they can
be dumped into your kidneys to be excreted in your urine as acetoacetate. The way to measure these excess
amounts of ketones is through a urine test strip, which changes color relative to the number of ketones in your
urine (usually the darker the purple color on the strip, the more ketones you have).
Unfortunately, this type of test is not always reliable. Once your body is in a keto-adapted state and you’re
efficiently using ketones for fuel, you will see progressively lower levels of ketones on the strip. This is
misleading: you may actually be in a deep state of ketosis and using almost all the ketones your body is
producing, but the strip says you have low ketones because there are fewer ketones spilling over into your urine.
So urine strips can be a cheap and effective testing method if you are just starting to get into ketosis, but they
aren’t viable for long-term testing once you’ve been consistently in ketosis.
Acetone (also called acetate) is the second ketone body and is produced by gas exchange in your lungs.
Acetone has been found in research to correlate very closely to levels of beta-hydroxybutyrate in the blood and
can be measured directly with a breath ketone meter. One of the key advantages of a breath meter for testing
ketones is that it is reusable and usually involves a one-time purchase of a device such as a Ketonix, Keyto, or
LEVL.
Finally, the primary ketone body that you use for energy (or can take as an exogenous ketone supplement) is
beta-hydroxybutyrate, or BHB. Here’s how BHB is used for energy: upon entering a cell, it is converted to
acetoacetone, which is ultimately converted to acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA is then used in the Krebs cycle for the
production of ATP.
A blood test for BHB can be done easily at home the same way people with diabetes check their blood
glucose. You simply prick your finger and squeeze a drop of blood onto a strip, and a small handheld reader tells
you the level of BHB in your blood. This is the most direct and accurate way to measure your level of ketones.
The downside to using a blood ketone meter is that some people may have a strong aversion to needles and
blood, and the testing strips are expensive, usually $5 to $10 per strip (although a newer device called Keto Mojo
has dropped the price of strips down to $0.99 each). The blood level of BHB is measured in millimoles, or mmol.
Studies have shown that the optimal ranges of BHB levels for ketosis are between 0.5 and 3.0 mmol, although
this varies based on activity levels, time in ketosis, fat-burning efficiency, and other factors. Other blood ketone
monitors include the Abbott Precision Xceed Pro, Precision Xtra (a meter that tests for both blood glucose and
ketones), and KetoSens.
So how do I test my ketones? Although I wear a CGM to monitor my blood glucose, I’m not a fan of the
hassle or expense of constantly measuring blood ketones. Instead, I use a device called a LEVL to monitor my
--- END PAGE 850 ---

--- PAGE 851 ---
breath ketones.
Clinical research has demonstrated a correlation between the amount of acetone detected in the breath,
blood ketone values, and body fat burned, making breath ketone testing a reliable indicator of ketosis fat loss. A
breath ketone–measuring device such as the LEVL detects trace amounts of acetone in your breath when your
body is burning fat. You simply breathe into it, and your breath is then analyzed by LEVL’s nanosensor, providing
you with an instant measurement of your body’s acetone concentration.
When you first shift into a lower carbohydrate intake, your body increases the amount of fat it burns relative
to the amount of carbohydrates, and your breath acetone concentration ramps up. This happens over the course
of three to seven days, until you reach an elevated level of breath acetone. If your diet becomes higher in calories
or carbohydrates, your body will become less dependent on fat for energy, resulting in a drop in acetone
concentration over one to two days.
I prefer this method of measuring ketones because it’s quick and easy. It does not measure blood mmol
concentrations but can be faster and more convenient than blood testing for ketones. A similar device is the
Lumen, which doesn’t measure ketones directly but approximates fat and carb burning based on carbon dioxide
it detects in the breath.
HOW TO TRACK YOUR STRESS
No one can perform at their best 24/7/365, because both mental and physical readiness varies from day to day.
This means some days are perfect for challenging your body and mind, and other days should be focused on easy,
restorative, relaxing activities. Ideally, this should be quantified and tracked. In chapter 12, I explained the idea of
a “readiness score,” which indicates how recovered you are and how well your body is responding to the
demands of daily life, and can give surprisingly accurate information about the potential onset of illness or injury
days before an actual problem occurs. It’s a sleek and efficient way to test the body’s recovery status and overall
wellness without the need for imprecise subjective evaluation, time-consuming questionnaires, or extensive
testing, and it requires just one simple piece of hardware: a wearable like a heart rate strap, ring, or wristband.
For example, I use the Oura ring readiness score as one of the few key daily metrics I glance at (the other is
sleep, and when I’m trying a new diet, food, or supplement, I keep an eye on my blood glucose and ketones). The
readiness score allows me to answer important questions such as these:
• Is my nervous system ready to take on the day?
• Should I take it easy today in my workouts or go all-out?
• How much stress can I handle today?
• Should I get extra sleep tonight, or take a nap today?
• Have recent lifestyle or environmental changes significantly affected me?
I can quickly answer all of these questions by glancing at my readiness score first thing in the morning. If my
daily stress load and recovery are in balance, then usually my readiness score is high. I use the same method with
the clients and athletes I coach to give me intelligent data that I use to structure their training for the week—
even occasionally pushing athletes in training through low periods of readiness followed by big bouts of recovery
so that they can super-compensate and bounce back even stronger (a training method called “periodization”).
It’s true that the state of your body and mind can give you subtle hints about your readiness. For example,
are you relaxed or tense? Is your mind crystal clear or covered in fog? Do you feel healthy or a bit under the
weather? But these are mainly subjective evaluations of your readiness. An objective evaluation is also
--- END PAGE 851 ---

--- PAGE 852 ---
important, which is why getting a personal readiness score is something I do each morning by glancing at the
smartphone app that connects to the Oura ring.
On the Oura ring, the readiness score ranges from 0 to 100 percent and is based on specific metrics tracked
by the ring, such as heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), sleep, body temperature, and the previous day’s
activities. A general rule is that if your readiness score is above 85 percent, you’re ready to meet the day’s more
stressful physical and mental challenges, and if it’s below 70 percent, you might want to consider concentrating
on recovery.
Of the metrics commonly used to determine readiness or stress score, the most important is HRV, which is a
measurement of the variance between heartbeats over a period of time. This measurement reflects the resilience
of your autonomic nervous system, which governs your ability to face and handle stress. Higher HRV scores are
correlated with resilient mood, better heart health, lower risk of early death, and improved recovery from
exercise and adaptability to stress. It’s important to understand that HRV scores aren’t necessarily
interchangeable between apps and devices, which means that a score of sixty on a wristband could be high, but
that same number measured by a ring or chest strap could indicate excessive stress. For this reason, it’s best to
simply look for patterns of increasing or decreasing HRV on whichever device you choose to use. In addition to
the Oura, a few other wearables that give good stress measurements are the Whoop and Biosensor wristbands,
the Hanu chest strap, and the Noise and Ultrahuman rings.
HOW TO TRACK YOUR SLEEP
What is the right amount of sleep for me? How fast did I fall asleep? Did I go through a normal series of sleep stages
during the night? Am I sleeping well? Until this new era of self-quantification came upon us, outside of sleep clinics,
it was very difficult to answer these questions objectively.
The problem with sleep monitoring is that traditionally, most people didn’t have tools with which to track
sleep accurately. Without a measuring device, you cannot really know whether you have had enough deep or
REM sleep. In addition, it can be tough to remember how well you slept, say, a couple weeks ago, or to generate a
realistic view of how your sleep trends with your diet, supplements, and exercise. This is important because your
“sleep history” can have a significant effect on your readiness score. In addition, it’s easy to misinterpret sleep
quality: having a feeling that you slept like a log doesn’t necessarily mean that your sleep was actually restorative,
and training through a low readiness score or sleep score can cause an impending injury or illness to rear its ugly
head, even if you subjectively felt as though you were ready for stress. I’ve seen this happen over and over again
both in myself and in clients and athletes I train who decided to just listen to their body instead of listening to
their body and using better self-quantification through science.
If you don’t know what your sleep quality is, you cannot act proactively. In the worst case, this can lead to a
situation where you start to learn more about your sleep only after you’ve developed some sort of sleep disorder,
such as severe sleep apnea or insomnia, and need to consult a sleep clinic or find yourself addicted to sleep
supplements or medications. Even if you do go to a professional sleep clinic or lab, you’re usually only there for a
night or two of sleep analysis, and the sleep-tracking devices there can be quite uncomfortable to wear, thus
giving you inaccurate data (go ahead, just try to get a normal night of sleep in a lab with a bunch of electrodes
attached to your head).
I’ve used the Oura ring as a simple yet unobtrusive sleep-tracking device: it doesn’t disturb sleep, but its
highly accurate sensors quietly measure body signals such as resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiration
rate, body temperature, and movement during sleep, along with tracking all your sleep cycles. You can grab your
sleep metrics in an easy-to-read format and visualizations from the smartphone app, along with guidance on
what the different metrics mean and how you can improve your sleep quality with time. Oura—along with many
--- END PAGE 852 ---

--- PAGE 853 ---
of the devices mentioned earlier in the stress section—uses the following parameters to calculate your sleep
score:•

Total sleep: This shows you the total amount of sleep you achieved the previous night, including light, REM,
and deep sleep. It’s important to realize that the total time you spent in bed does not necessarily equate to
the total amount of sleep you got.•

Efficiency: Put simply, efficiency means the percentage of time you spent sleeping while in bed. The longer
you slept, the more efficient your sleep was. In general, a sleep efficiency score of 85 percent or above shows
that you fell asleep quickly enough (in less than twenty minutes) and didn’t wake up too often during the
night.•

Disturbances: Disturbances are the other side of the efficiency coin and show the total time you spent awake
during the night. Disturbances such as wake-ups, get-ups, and restless time during sleep can have a big
influence on your sleep quality, resulting in less-restorative sleep. This can be one of the primary reasons
behind daytime sleepiness. Obviously, many things can cause your sleep to be interrupted, but variables such
as stress, noise, sleep companions, light, room temperature, infections, drinking too much (alcohol or even
water) so that you get up to pee during the night, and later evening activities (exercise, screen time, heavy
meals) are all on the list of suspects.•

REM sleep: As you know from chapter 7, REM is short for “rapid eye movement.” This is the stage of sleep
that is associated with dreaming, memory consolidation, learning, and creativity. It ideally makes up 20 to 25
percent of your total sleep time, but that percentage tends to decrease with age.•

Deep sleep: Deep sleep, or NREM sleep, is considered the most restorative and rejuvenating stage of sleep.
This is the stage when muscle repair and growth takes place, your body is relaxed, your blood pressure is
lower, and it’s harder to wake you up. The amount of deep sleep varies between nights and individuals, but
on average, adults should spend 15 to 20 percent of their total sleep time in deep sleep. This percentage also
tends to decrease with age. Simple practices such as daily physical activity and avoidance of heavy meals and
alcohol before bedtime, long naps, and caffeine in the afternoon can increase your amount of deep sleep, as
can following all the sleep hygiene tips in chapter 7, such as sleeping in a cool, dark room with limited sound
interruptions.•

Sleep latency: This is the amount of time it takes for you to fall to sleep. Sleep latency is highly variable, but
it shouldn’t take you more than fifteen to twenty minutes to fall asleep. There are many reasons that your
sleep latency might decrease, including exposure to too much blue light at night, a late dinner, and
consumption of alcohol too close to bedtime. Bear in mind, too, that dozing off in less than five minutes can
often indicate that you are sleep-deprived or that you didn’t sleep enough the previous night.•

Sleep timing: As you learned in chapter 7, every human has a biological clock aligned to day and night cycles.
All of our essential biological processes, such as body temperature, hormone releases, and hunger, operate on
twenty-four-hour cycles known as the circadian rhythms. As you also learned in that chapter, there are
significant differences in our rhythms. Some of us are morning oriented, some are evening people, and others
are somewhere in-between. But regardless of orientation, having consistency in your rhythm and your sleep
timing is important (for example, I go to bed at approximately 10 p.m. most nights and am up at
approximately 6 a.m. most mornings). In addition, having the midpoint of your sleep land somewhere
between midnight and 3 a.m. is preferable from a sleep quality point of view.
The Oura ring uses all these parameters to calculate your daily sleep score, which ranges from 0 to 100
percent. As a rule of thumb, the higher it is, the better and more restorative your sleep.
--- END PAGE 853 ---

--- PAGE 854 ---
Finally, although many wearables don’t yet incorporate blood oxygen sensing into the overall sleep score,
they do allow for measurement of blood oxygen during sleep. For example, the Oura ring measures peripheral
oxygen saturation (SpO ) levels in your blood while you sleep by sending light from the ring’s red and infrared
2LEDs into your finger and then measuring how much light is reflected. Richly oxygenated blood reflects more
red light than infrared light, while poorly oxygenated blood reflects more infrared light than red light. When
combined with measurements of respiration rate, or the use of a nighttime noise-monitoring app like
SleepSpace, this data can give you incredibly helpful clues about whether you may have one of the most serious
but less discussed causes of poor sleep and daytime tiredness: sleep apnea.
How I Use My Sleep Data
Let’s take a look at how to practically use the data you can glean from a sleep system like the Oura, shall we? Before
writing this chapter, I opened up all my app data. Two nights ago, I was in bed from 10:31 p.m. until 7:29 a.m. Pretty
impressive, eh? Makes me look like a good little sleeper. But upon taking a closer look at my sleep data, I can identify a
few concerning issues, including these:
• I spent a good hour of that time awake.
• I spent five hours and thirteen minutes of that time in light sleep (59 percent of the total night of sleep!).
• My lowest resting heart rate of 39 bpm occurred at about 4:30 a.m., nearly two hours later than my lowest rate
normally occurs, and was three beats higher than my normal lowest resting heart rate of 36 bpm.
So, although one would think upon first glance that I had a rock-star night of sleep, that’s far from the truth. As a
matter of fact, this morning I received a warning that my readiness score is low and that I may not be recovered fully
from the previous day’s activity. Interestingly, the previous day’s activity was a three-hour horseback ride, an activity
my body definitely was not used to and which it needed additional time to recover from.
Pretty interesting, eh?
By adjusting my activities the next night—avoiding screen time after 9 p.m., eating a light dinner, not drinking a second
glass of wine, and taking a magnesium bath to both relax me and bring my core temperature down—I achieved a sleep
score of 97 percent, with my lowest heart rate during sleep being 34 bpm (nice and low for me), achieved at my ideal
time of 2:30 a.m. I spent 27 percent of the night in deep sleep and only 5 percent awake, and the next day my Oura
--- END PAGE 854 ---

--- PAGE 855 ---
app even congratulated me for sleeping “like a bear in the winter.” I had a high readiness score and high physical
activity recommendation for the day.
HOW TO TEST YOUR FITNESS
What gets measured gets managed, and because of that, I’ve always been able to gather a great deal of motivation
to stay in shape by regularly testing specific parameters of overall fitness and activity. There’s just something
about knowing you need to step out after dinner to take an extra thousand steps to hit your 10K daily step count
goal, you need to crank out a few extra pull-ups so that you have beaten your dead hang-time test, or you need to
back off the cookies so that your visceral fat score drops.
Here are the most important daily and monthly variables to pay attention to when it comes to your body.
Step Count
Frequency: daily
Measuring your step count is easily accomplished with the use of a wearable activity tracker, smartphone
app, or pedometer. These devices typically use accelerometers to detect movement and count the number of
steps taken throughout the day. Wearable activity trackers are worn on the wrist, while pedometers can be
clipped onto clothing or carried in a pocket. Smartphone apps often utilize the built-in accelerometer and GPS
features to track steps and provide additional insights such as distance traveled and calories burned.
Research suggests that achieving a daily step count of at least 10,000 is associated with various health
benefits, including improved cardiovascular health, weight management, and overall well-being. By using an
office treadmill, walking just about anywhere I can, taking the stairs, parking in the far corners of parking lots,
and stopping regularly during the workday to move, my average daily step count in the past year was 16,778!
Once you start measuring, you may be surprised at how few steps you actually take and how tiny modifications
--- END PAGE 855 ---

--- PAGE 856 ---
to your day can add up quickly. Maintaining a high walking speed is also important, as smaller declines in
walking speed are associated with slower aging rates.
VO Max2 
Frequency: monthly
As you may recall from chapter 10, VO max is the number of milliliters of oxygen per kilogram, per minute
2 that your body uses in your mitochondria to create ATP. It is a score of how well your whole body is working to
extract oxygen and use it productively, and it gives you information about lung capacity, the capacity of oxygen
to diffuse across the lungs and alveoli into blood, the ability of the heart to pump blood into tissues, the ability of
tissues to extract blood into muscle, and the ability of the muscle to use oxygen and produce ATP. Higher VO2
max levels are also associated with better verbal short-term memory.
Although many wearables will approximate your VO max based on your workout pace and heart rate, the
2 Cooper 12-minute run test is a simple, verified way to regularly track your VO max. This test requires you to run
2 or walk as far as possible in a 12-minute period and is usually carried out on a running track with cones placed at
various distances to enable measuring of the distance. The objective is to measure the maximum distance
covered during the 12-minute period. There is also a 3-mile cycling version of the test for those who can’t or
don’t like to run.
The Cooper test is simple: after a brief warm-up, you record the total number of miles or kilometers you
travel in exactly 12 minutes. This test is designed to be conducted on a track with a clearly marked distance. You
can perform the test on a treadmill, but be sure to raise the incline to 1 degree to simulate outdoor running. To
calculate your estimated VO max results (in ml/kg/min), use either of these formulas:2 
Kilometers: VO max = (22.351 × kilometers) – 11.2882 
Miles: VO max = (35.97 × miles) – 11.291
2 The easiest way to get your test results (your VO max score) and compare yourself to others of your age and
2 gender is with an online test results calculator, which I’ll include on the resources page for this chapter. After
completing the test, you can compare your results to the norms and recommendations for your age and gender,
which I’ll also include on the resources page.
If you want a more precise measurement of VO max, you can use a portable VO analyzer like the VO2
2 2 Master, which allows for portable metabolic testing with a surprising degree of accuracy and minimal,
lightweight equipment.
Strength
Frequency: monthly
A simple way to regularly test strength is with a hand grip dynamometer. Grip strength refers to the force
exerted by the muscles of your hand when gripping an object, but it is actually an indicator of both hand and
forearm muscle health and is recognized as a surrogate marker for overall muscular strength. Many studies have
shown the association of grip strength with various health outcomes, including cardiovascular disease, mobility,
cognitive function, and overall mortality. A decline in grip strength can be a predictor of increasing frailty and
reduced life expectancy, making it a valuable tool for gauging your overall health and potential longevity.
One study of over 500,000 adults between ages forty and sixty-nine correlated grip strength to rates of
healthy outcomes for diseases ranging from heart disease to respiratory illness and even cancer. It found that a
grip strength measurement of less than 57 pounds for men or less than 35 pounds for women was associated with
“higher overall risk of death and higher risk for specific illnesses.”
--- END PAGE 856 ---

--- PAGE 857 ---

approximate values to get an idea of where your strength lies. It’s also ideal to have no more than a 10 percent
differential between hands.

*Note from Ben: I’m a bigger fan of a push-up test for push strength, which is basically doing as many push-
