THE BOUNDLESS DIET
There are a host of diets out there that are designed to optimize health,
and which one will work best for you depends entirely on your
biochemical individuality. Here, I’ve compiled the best of these diets and
grouped them into beginner, intermediate, and advanced categories based
on a trajectory from a very clean and somewhat restrictive reset diet to a
more liberal eating plan with a larger selection of foods, and finally to a
widely varied diet that’s easy to sustain for life. In other words, unlike in
the exercise program, the beginner, intermediate, and advanced categories
have nothing to do with how difficult a diet is; it’s all about taking you
--- END PAGE 1283 ---

--- PAGE 1284 ---
from a standard American diet to a more ancestral, health-optimizing,
widely varied way of eating.
For each diet, I’ve listed test results and symptoms that may make the
diet the right one for you, and I’ve provided a sample day of meals for
each. If you’ve read chapters 13 and 14 and done much of the self-
quantification from chapter 16, you are already equipped with most of the
information you need to customize your diet, but if you’re looking for
something “done-for-you,” these protocols will give you plenty to work
with.
No matter which diet you decide to pursue, make sure you adhere to
the following principles:
• Incorporate regular intermittent fasts or longer fasting periods.
• Ruthlessly eliminate inflammatory foods and control glycemic
variability.
• Rather than engaging in long-term calorie and carbohydrate
restriction, occasionally refeed your body with adequate calories and
carbohydrates.
• Occasionally engage in periods of more intense detoxification.
• Whenever given the option between real food and packaged or
processed food, choose the former.
• Eat a very wide variety of multicolored plants, bitters, herbs, and
spices.
• Whenever possible, choose clean, organic, wild, non-GMO foods and
ingredients.
• Whenever possible, eat locally grown in-season foods.
• Chew food thoroughly, and eat in a relaxed, grateful parasympathetic
state.
--- END PAGE 1284 ---

--- PAGE 1285 ---
• Review the longevity tips in chapter 19 and incorporate those key
principles into your diet as often as possible.
Beginner
The diets in this beginner section are clean eating protocols that aren’t
meant to be followed permanently, but instead temporarily implemented
for cleansing, detoxification, and preparing for a less restrictive diet after
one to twelve weeks. These are somewhat restrictive plans that I do not
necessarily recommend following for life unless you have a serious
condition such as celiac or Crohn’s disease or severe food allergies.
If you’ve been eating a diet or living a toxic or unhealthy lifestyle that
has caused gut damage, inflammation, sugar dependency, or similar gut
problems, I recommend that you follow any of the diets in this section
before progressing to an intermediate plan. If you have more serious gut
issues, autoimmune symptoms, or a condition like dysbiosis, stick to this
type of diet until your symptoms subside, which sometimes takes up to six
months. (In the case of the GAPS diet, it is recommended that you follow
it for up to two years to fully heal a leaky gut.) If you need to detox or
cleanse at any point throughout the year, you can return to one of these
diets—for example, you can perform a one-to-two-week liver cleanse in
the spring and winter or follow an Elemental Diet for the first thirty days
of each year.
Ultimately, rather than recommending one single diet—which you
know from chapter 14 is a flawed approach—I’m equipping you with a
number of diets that you can use to heal your gut, ease digestion, detox
your body, and prepare your digestive system for more variety.
AUTOIMMUNE PALEO (AIP) DIET
--- END PAGE 1285 ---

--- PAGE 1286 ---
Also known as the Paleo autoimmune protocol, the AIP diet is a much
stricter version of the Paleo diet (which is based on meat, fish, vegetables,
nuts, and seeds). It eliminates dairy, grains, eggs, nightshades, legumes,
and other foods that may cause inflammation in people with a leaky gut.
As explained in chapter 13, leaky gut can lead to an autoimmune response
in which your own immune system tags your tissues, such as your eyes or
nervous system, with certain types of antibodies, including those listed
below. This falsely signals to your immune system that those tissues are
foreign invaders, and your immune system then attacks those tissues.
Each autoimmune disease also has markers specific to that condition, and
BoundlessBook.com/21 includes more information on which antibodies
are specific to which diseases. By focusing on nutrient-rich foods and
avoiding inflammatory ones, the AIP diet aims to heal inflammation and
any holes in the gut.
People who follow the AIP diet typically should follow it strictly for
four to eight weeks and then slowly reintroduce foods that they have been
avoiding. The best book to accompany this diet is The Autoimmune Paleo
Cookbook by Mickey Trescott, since it has a host of tasty recipes that don’t
taste like cardboard. After you’ve spent at least four to eight weeks on one
of the diets in this section, the Wahls Protocol (outlined in the
intermediate section) is also an excellent diet for managing autoimmunity
long term.
You may be a good candidate for the AIP diet if you have elevated
antibodies as indicated by an autoimmune blood test, leaky gut syndrome,
or a diagnosed autoimmune condition. Basic symptoms suggestive of
autoimmune disease can also include chronic fatigue; joint pain or
stiffness; muscle weakness; skin rashes; gastrointestinal symptoms such as
bloating, diarrhea, or constipation; and systemic inflammation. Blood tests
may reveal markers of autoimmune activity, such as elevated levels of
antibodies directed against specific tissues or organs, like anti-nuclear
--- END PAGE 1286 ---

--- PAGE 1287 ---
antibodies (ANA), anti-thyroid antibodies (e.g., anti-TPO, anti-Tg), anti-
citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), or anti-tissue transglutaminase
antibodies (anti-tTG). Genetic testing may identify specific gene
variations associated with autoimmune susceptibility, such as HLA-DQ2
and HLA-DQ8 for celiac disease or specific human leukocyte antigen
(HLA) alleles for autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or type
1 diabetes. Gut testing, such as comprehensive stool analysis or intestinal
permeability testing, may reveal imbalances in gut microbiota, intestinal
inflammation, or increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), which are
commonly associated with autoimmune conditions. Urine testing may
assess levels of specific metabolites or inflammatory markers, providing
additional insight into immune function and systemic inflammation.

SPECIFIC CARBOHYDRATE DIET (SCD)
The Specific Carbohydrate Diet (SCD) was first described by Sidney V.
Haas in 1924 as a way to treat celiac disease and was further refined in the
1951 medical textbook The Management of Celiac Disease. It was later
repopularized in 1987 by Elaine Gottschall, the mother of one of Haas’s
patients.
The SCD is a gluten-free and grain-free diet and was a popular
treatment for celiac disease decades before gluten was even discovered.
--- END PAGE 1287 ---

--- PAGE 1288 ---
The diet eliminates complex carbohydrates such as grains, starches, most
dairy products, sugars, and processed foods while emphasizing nutrient-
dense foods that are easily digested and absorbed, including lean proteins,
certain fruits, nonstarchy vegetables, nuts, and healthy fats. By reducing
the intake of fermentable carbohydrates that can fuel pathogenic bacteria
and promote inflammation in the gut, the SCD aims to restore balance to
the gut microbiota, reduce intestinal inflammation, improve digestive
function, and alleviate symptoms. It may be supplemented with
probiotics, digestive enzymes, and other gut-supportive nutrients to
further enhance gut healing and optimize digestive health.
I recommend you follow this plan if you have IBD, IBS, bloating, gas,
or gut inflammation, particularly if these issues are brought on by gluten
or grain consumption. The best book to accompany the SCD program is
Gotschall’s Breaking the Vicious Cycle.
Symptoms of conditions that may benefit from the SCD diet include
chronic gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating,
diarrhea, and/or constipation, as well as systemic symptoms such as
fatigue, joint pain, and weight loss. Blood tests may reveal markers of
inflammation, such as elevated levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) or fecal
calprotectin, which are commonly associated with inflammatory bowel
diseases like Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. Genetic testing may
identify specific gene variations associated with increased susceptibility to
IBD, such as NOD2/CARD15 mutations. Gut testing, including
comprehensive stool analysis or microbial profiling, may uncover
imbalances in gut microbiota, dysbiosis, intestinal inflammation, or
increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), which are common features
of conditions like IBD, IBS, and other gastrointestinal disorders. Urine
testing may assess levels of specific metabolites or inflammatory markers,
providing additional insights into gut health and systemic inflammation.
--- END PAGE 1288 ---

--- PAGE 1289 ---
Based on these assessments, individuals with confirmed or suspected
gastrointestinal conditions such as IBD, IBS, or celiac disease and related
symptoms may benefit from following the SCD.

BoundlessBook.com/21.

GUT AND PSYCHOLOGY SYNDROME (GAPS) DIET
Dr. Natasha Campbell-McBride, a neurologist and nutritionist, developed
the GAPS diet and wrote the book Gut and Psychology Syndrome to assist
her patients—especially children—who were experiencing problematic
gut-brain issues. Like the SCD, the GAPS diet removes potentially
problematic foods, particularly grains and gluten-containing foods, but it
also focuses on adding healing, nutrient-dense foods. If you have cognitive
issues, irritation, brain fog, or nervous system–based problems affected by
the gut, such as ADHD, this can be a good program to follow.
The diet emphasizes nutrient-dense whole foods that are easily
digested and absorbed, while eliminating potentially inflammatory or
allergenic foods that may contribute to gut dysbiosis and inflammation. It
typically involves three stages: the Introduction diet, which focuses on
healing and sealing the gut lining; the Full GAPS diet, which includes a
wider variety of foods while continuing to support gut health; and the
Maintenance diet, which is tailored to individual needs and focuses on
long-term gut maintenance and overall health. By removing potentially
--- END PAGE 1289 ---

--- PAGE 1290 ---
harmful foods and incorporating gut-healing foods such as bone broth,
fermented foods, and nutrient-dense vegetables, fruits, and healthy fats,
the GAPS diet aims to reduce inflammation, support digestive function,
and improve neurological and psychological symptoms. It may be
supplemented with probiotics, digestive enzymes, and other gut-
supportive nutrients to further enhance gut healing and optimize overall
health and well-being.
Symptoms of conditions that may benefit from the GAPS diet include
gastrointestinal issues such as chronic bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhea,
and constipation, as well as neurological or psychological symptoms such
as anxiety, depression, mood swings, and cognitive difficulties. Blood tests
may reveal markers of inflammation or immune dysregulation, such as
elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines or antibodies, which are
commonly associated with conditions like IBS, IBD, autoimmune
disorders, and neurological or psychiatric conditions. Genetic testing may
identify specific gene variations associated with increased susceptibility to
gut dysbiosis, inflammation, and neurological or psychiatric disorders. Gut
testing, such as comprehensive stool analysis or intestinal permeability
testing, may uncover imbalances in gut microbiota, dysbiosis, intestinal
inflammation, or increased gut permeability (leaky gut), which are
common features of conditions like IBS, IBD, SIBO, and other
gastrointestinal and neurological disorders. Urine testing may assess
levels of specific metabolites or neurotransmitters, providing additional
insights into gut health, neurotransmitter balance, and systemic
inflammation.

SWISS DETOX DIET / COLORADO CLEANSE
Both the Swiss Detox Diet, developed by Dr. Thomas Rau, and the

Body, Mind, and Sport.

incorporates the Swiss Detox Diet. I’ve been to this facility for a complete
colon and liver detox, which combines European biological medicine
practices with a detox diet for treatment of excessive toxins and also
Lyme, Parkinson’s, mold and mycotoxin overload, cancer, and beyond.
You may want to follow this diet as a brief one-to-two-week cleanse if

and/or difficulty with bowel movements and generally want a done-for-
--- END PAGE 1291 ---

--- PAGE 1292 ---
you short-term cleansing approach particularly relevant to liver and
gallbladder function. For example, low or high levels of alanine

albumin, or gamma-glutamyl transferase can all be measured on a blood

CARNIVORE DIET
In chapter 14, I described my approach to and experience with the
carnivore diet. The diet originated in the early 1900s with an Arctic
explorer named Vilhjalmur Stefansson, who noticed a near-complete
absence of chronic diseases in the Inuit culture, where the diet consisted
entirely of meats and animal fats. He subsequently began experimenting
with an all-meat diet, consuming nothing but meat and water for a year,
and experienced noticeable results in his overall health and vitality.
The carnivore diet is a meat-based diet that excludes all sources of
carbohydrates. It is restrictive, allowing only proteins (beef, chicken, pork,
and some fish), animal fats (primarily from the above meat sources), and
--- END PAGE 1292 ---

--- PAGE 1293 ---
organ meats (such as liver, kidney, and bone marrow). Other animal foods
like dairy and eggs can also be consumed, and eating all animal parts such
as organs, cartilage, and bones is encouraged. Off-limits foods include nuts
and seeds, legumes, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and all other plant-
based foods.
While there are no clinical trials that assess the benefits of an all-meat
diet, a 2021 survey involving over 2,000 participants who had been on a
carnivore diet for at least six months showed self-reported improvements
in sleep disruption, fatigue, brain fog, cognition, and mental clarity, being
overweight or underweight, blood sugar dysregulation (type 1 and 2
diabetes and metabolic syndrome), autoimmunity, joint and muscle pain,
mental health, skin issues, and urinary difficulties.
I typically only recommend the carnivore diet as a short-term stint to
heal the gut, which can happen when you eliminate all plant defense
compounds and simplify the confusion of figuring out what’s aggravating
you by eliminating just about everything—except meat. Despite the fact
that modern humans are omnivores, proponents of the carnivore meal
plan believe that it is completely safe to stay on long term. However, if you
choose to do so, you must incorporate organ meats into your diet to avoid
becoming deficient in certain nutrients, like B vitamins and vitamin C.
Many folks who transition to this diet begin with a modified approach
of intermittent fasting and including foods like honey, berries, squash, and
cucumber (which is low in lectins and oxalates). If you still experience
symptoms on the carnivore diet, it could be a reaction to eggs, lactose, or
fish, which you can also eliminate, but if you do, you need to include an
iodine source, like iodized salt.
Finally, the carnivore diet is ketogenic, and you may experience keto
adaptation (“keto flu”) during the first two to four weeks, which can cause
side effects like gas, bloating, abdominal pain, and loose stool due to the
natural shift in the gut microbiome that occurs when switching to a low-
--- END PAGE 1293 ---

--- PAGE 1294 ---
carb diet. In this case, supplementing with electrolyte powders or drinks
that contain sodium, potassium, and magnesium can help.
People who might benefit from a carnivore diet often report chronic
digestive issues, autoimmune conditions, or inflammatory diseases that
have not responded well to other dietary interventions. Symptoms such as
bloating, gas, joint pain, skin issues, and fatigue that persist despite trying
other diets might suggest that this more “radical” dietary change could be
beneficial.
Blood tests that might indicate a carnivore diet could be a good fit
include high levels of inflammation markers (such as C-reactive protein),
unresolved deficiencies in B and iron (despite supplementation),
12 autoimmune or food allergy issues (particularly sensitivities to grains,
grasses, legumes, etc.), and lipid profiles that suggest an intolerance to
carbohydrates (for example, elevated triglycerides and low HDL
cholesterol). Additionally, insulin resistance markers like fasting glucose
and HbA1c levels might guide a recommendation to make this shift.
Genetic testing can provide insight into how well someone might tolerate
a carnivore diet. For instance, individuals with genetic predispositions to
undermethylation may do better on a lower-plant, higher-meat diet, as
would individuals who have an ancestral history of higher amounts of
meat and fish rather than vegetables and fruits. People who clear large
amounts of LDL particles due to favorable PCSK9 genes may do better on
a carnivore diet.

SIBO BI-PHASIC DIET (B-PD)
SIBO stands for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and it is
characterized by the excessive growth of bacteria in the small intestine.
This condition can result from various factors, including maldigestion,
malabsorption, and a leaky gut. It can cause digestive and extraintestinal
symptoms such as bloating, gas, abdominal pain, heartburn, constipation,
diarrhea, rashes, headaches, and fatigue.
The SIBO Bi-Phasic Diet (SIBO B-PD) was developed by Dr. Nirala
Jacobi to manage and treat SIBO, and it is one of the best systematic
dietary approaches to eliminating gas and bloating when something like
the SCD or basic low-FODMAP diet doesn’t seem to be working. It
combines principles of the low-FODMAP and SCD diets and is divided
into two phases. The first phase restricts dietary fermentable
carbohydrates (high-FODMAP foods like certain fruits, vegetables, grains,
legumes, dairy products, sweeteners, and food additives) to reduce
bacterial overgrowth and their production of metabolic by-products,
relieve SIBO symptoms, heal the gut, and restore optimal digestive
function. The second phase introduces antimicrobial agents to remove any
remaining bacterial overgrowth while reintroducing foods into the diet.
This phase also helps you identify trigger foods and maintain a healthy and
balanced diet that supports gut health and prevents the recurrence of
SIBO in the long term.
Phase 1 of the SIBO B-PD lasts two to six weeks and involves avoiding
or minimizing intake of foods high in fermentable carbohydrates that can
ferment in the gut and exacerbate symptoms. This restrictive phase of the
--- END PAGE 1295 ---

--- PAGE 1296 ---
diet emphasizes eating smaller, more frequent meals with adequate
protein and healthy fat sources. Choices during this phase include•

Protein: poultry, beef, lamb, pork, fish, eggs•

Nonstarchy vegetables: leafy greens, zucchini, bell peppers,
cucumbers, carrots, eggplant, bok choy•

Healthy fats: olive oil, coconut oil, avocado, moderate amounts of nuts
and seeds•

Fruits: lemon, lime, berries•

Fermented foods (as tolerated): cultured vegetables, sauerkraut,
kimchi•

Beverages: water, herbal teas, black coffee
Phase 2, the reintroduction phase, lasts four to six weeks. The
objective here is to gradually reintroduce foods to expand the diet and
identify individual dietary triggers. Phase 2 naturally progresses into the
final phase of the SIBO B-PD—the maintenance phase. The overall goal of
the SIBO B-PD protocol is to create a sustainable, nutritious, and
individualized dietary plan based on your tolerance levels.
Basic symptoms suggestive of SIBO and a potential benefit of this B-
PD diet include chronic bloating, abdominal pain or discomfort, gas,
diarrhea, constipation, and nutrient malabsorption. Blood tests may reveal
markers of inflammation, such as elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) or
erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), as well as deficiencies in certain
vitamins or minerals due to malabsorption. Genetic testing may uncover
gene variations associated with impaired gut motility or immune function,
predisposing you to SIBO. Gut testing, such as breath testing for hydrogen
and methane gases, can confirm the presence of SIBO by detecting
abnormal levels of these gases produced by bacteria in the small intestine.
Urine testing may reveal elevated levels of certain metabolites associated
--- END PAGE 1296 ---

--- PAGE 1297 ---
with bacterial overgrowth or gut dysbiosis, further supporting the
diagnosis of SIBO. A comprehensive stool test can also assess gut health
by measuring markers that signal inflammation, intestinal permeability,
dysbiosis, intestinal infection, and maldigestion.
A SIBO breath test, or the use of an at-home Food Marble device for
breath testing, can monitor your SIBO treatment progress and confirm
SIBO eradication by tracking changes in hydrogen, methane, and hydrogen
sulfide gas levels.

ELEMENTAL DIET
Should you need to pull out all the stops to manage gut inflammation,
SIBO, candida, yeast, fungus, constipation, FODMAP sensitivities, or leaky
gut, or if you simply want to push the reset button on what seems to be
problematic digestion, you can spend one to four weeks on an elemental
diet. It’s a good choice if you have the indicators of SIBO or FODMAP
sensitivities, but no other solution, including any other diet in this
chapter, seems to be working.
--- END PAGE 1297 ---

--- PAGE 1298 ---
Warning: This diet is highly restrictive and only appropriate for a quick
one-week to one-month stint. The elemental diet is the simplest and,
admittedly, most boring of all the beginner diet options. It involves
consuming a meal replacement formula for breakfast, lunch, and dinner,
along with a few extra oils, fats, and amino acids for added nutrients. For a
meal replacement drink, I recommend one or two servings of Thorne’s
Mediclear SGS or Dr. Ruscio’s Elemental Health formula. For extra
protein, fat, and calories, you can blend the formula with bone broth
and/or add 10 to 20 g essential amino acids to each shake, along with a
teaspoon or tablespoon of extra-virgin olive oil and MCT or coconut oil.
These formulas are expensive, so you can also use my DIY version of
an elemental health smoothie, which tastes like an orange creamsicle
(though you may still tire of orange creamsicles after a month!). Blend the
following: ice and organic coconut water to the desired texture, a liquid
multivitamin (Mary Ruth’s is good), 10 g essential amino acids (mango
flavor Kion Aminos works well for this recipe), a dash of natural vanilla
extract, a pinch of salt, a tablespoon of honey, and an ounce of extra-virgin
olive oil. I’ll include a video of me making it on the resources page for this
chapter.
Should you want even more variety, you can include soups, broths, and
steamed vegetables in your evening meal. To learn more about the
elemental diet and what can and cannot be included, I recommend Dr.
Allison Siebecker’s website, SIBOInfo.com.

Intermediate
After you follow any of the beginner diets for eight to twelve weeks, your
gut should be ready for a wider variety of foods. In this section, I’ll
introduce you to my favorite diets that are clean and easy to digest and
consist primarily of real, whole foods.
Many of the diets in this section tend to be low-carbohydrate or
ketogenic. This is not because a ketogenic diet is perfect for everyone but
because eating carbohydrates throughout the day can lead to blood sugar
fluctuations and inflammation. A low-carbohydrate or ketogenic approach
is a good way to avoid this, and most people have the most stable energy
levels when they consume no more than around 30 percent of their
calories from carbohydrates, especially starches and sugars.
For athletes, extremely active individuals, folks with the AMY1 gene
variant (which allows them to consume more carbohydrates), and people
who need more carbohydrates, I do recommend prioritizing the addition
of extra nightly carbohydrates to the diets in this section. In this type of
“refeed” scenario, you can add 50 to 250 g (depending on your size and
activity level) of clean starches in the form of sweet potatoes, yams, taro,
other tubers, parsnips, carrots, beets, rice, or properly prepared (either
soaked, sprouted, or fermented) grains, with foods such as dark chocolate,
berries, or coconut or organic dairy ice cream for dessert. Highly active
individuals may also benefit from a weekly carbohydrate refeed scenario, a
day on which carbs make up about 40 percent of your daily caloric intake.
WAHLS PROTOCOL (LOW-CARB VERSION)
--- END PAGE 1299 ---

--- PAGE 1300 ---
After being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), Dr. Terry Wahls began
studying food and vitamins and created a nutrient-rich, Paleo-esque diet.
Within a year of changing her way of eating, she was out of her wheelchair
and biking miles at a time. The best book to read to learn more about this
plan is her book The Wahls Protocol.
On the Wahls Protocol, you eat lots of meat and fish, vegetables
(especially green, leafy ones), brightly colored fruit like berries, and fat
from animal and plant sources (especially omega-3 fatty acids), and you
avoid dairy, eggs, grain, legumes, nightshades, and sugar. The low-carb
version of the Wahls Protocol is especially good for managing
autoimmune conditions while introducing a bit more variety than the AIP.
This diet can also work well for those with mast cell issues aggravated
by mold and mycotoxins or Lyme, and for those with mitochondrial
dysfunction or poor nervous system health. Symptoms of conditions that
may benefit from the Wahls Protocol include chronic fatigue, muscle
weakness, cognitive difficulties, mood disturbances, and neurological
symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or balance problems. From a
testing standpoint, blood tests may reveal markers of inflammation or
immune dysregulation, such as elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines,
autoimmune antibodies, or markers of oxidative stress, which are
commonly associated with autoimmune conditions, neurological
disorders, and chronic inflammatory conditions. Genetic testing may
identify specific gene variations associated with increased susceptibility to
oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and
neurological or autoimmune disorders. Gut testing, such as
comprehensive stool analysis or microbial profiling, may uncover
imbalances in gut microbiota, dysbiosis, intestinal inflammation, or
increased intestinal permeability (leaky gut), which are common features
of conditions like IBD, IBS, SIBO, and other gastrointestinal and
autoimmune disorders. Urine testing can also show increased levels of
--- END PAGE 1300 ---

--- PAGE 1301 ---
specific metabolites related to inflammatory markers that suggest
impairments in mitochondrial function, oxidative stress, and systemic
inflammation. Based on assessments like this, if you have confirmed or
suspected autoimmune, neurological, or chronic inflammatory conditions,
you may benefit from following the Wahls Protocol.

PLANT PARADOX DIET
The Plant Paradox diet, developed by Dr. Stephen Gundry and described
in his book The Plant Paradox, eliminates lectins (a natural plant-based
defensive protein that can cause gastric distress in many people and is
found in foods such as green beans, lentils, and edamame) and limits
sugar and polyunsaturated omega-6 fats. It also limits phytates, which are
a source of energy for sprouting seeds; when people eat them in plants (as
phytic acid), they bind to nutrients like manganese, iron, and zinc, making
them indigestible and increasing your risk of being deficient in those
minerals.
The Plant Paradox diet usually starts with a three-day cleanse, during
which you repopulate your gut bacteria with leafy greens, cruciferous
vegetables, clean protein, and good fats, and then has a second phase in
which you eat only from the list of approved foods for at least six weeks.
On the resources page for this chapter, I’ve simplified the diet to skip the
--- END PAGE 1301 ---

--- PAGE 1302 ---
two phases and still give you a lectin-free protocol; this version also uses a
ketogenic strategy to control blood sugar.
I recommend this diet if you want to eat a rich variety of vegetables
but have difficulty digesting them and are sensitive to lectins, phytates,
oxalates, and other built-in plant defense mechanisms—it lets you
consume a diverse array of plants prepared in a manner that makes them
easier to digest. It’s a good choice if you have indicators of plant-, legume-,
or grain-digesting issues, such as gluten sensitivities, IBS, or other
problematic responses to nuts, seeds, and legumes. Many mineral
deficiency symptoms can occur due to phytates, including paleness,
dizziness, dry hair and skin, restless legs, anxiety, headaches, and fatigue
(iron deficiency); diarrhea, hair loss, poor immune function, and loss of
appetite (zinc deficiency); or low fertility and impaired glucose tolerance
(manganese deficiency). You may also have markers of inflammation or
autoimmune issues such as low levels of blood TNF-alpha, adiponectin, or
interleukin-6; a low white blood cell count; low ferritin; or low T3. These,
along with a food allergy and intolerance test (see chapter 16), can give
you insight into whether modulating plant intake may be a good idea for
you.

PALEO DIET
--- END PAGE 1302 ---

--- PAGE 1303 ---
The Paleo diet is flexible and can be adapted for your specific needs, but it
essentially cuts out modern agricultural foods that can cause an
inflammatory reaction in many people and focuses on foods that our
Paleolithic ancestors would likely have eaten, depending on seasonal
availability.
One of the fundamental concepts behind Paleo is that humans were
hunter-gatherers far longer than they’ve been farmers and cultivators. As a
result, our genes evolved to favor the nutrient-dense plants and meats of
those hunter-gatherers, not the high-sugar, high-dairy, high-refined-carb
modern Western diet.
The standard Paleo diet includes meat (especially organ meats like
liver and kidneys, bone broth, and marrow); high-quality animal fats;
seafood; eggs (ideally, pasture-raised); nonstarchy vegetables; low-
glycemic-index fruits like berries, citrus, and stone fruits; coconut oil,
olive oil, and avocado oil; nuts and seeds; and herbs and spices. The
inflammatory foods excluded from the Paleo diet include grains like
wheat, barley, oats, corn, and rice; dairy; refined sugar; processed foods;
and vegetable oils (such as soybean, peanut, corn, and canola oils). Foods
that are eaten in moderate amounts (if they are well-tolerated) include
legumes like lentils and chickpeas and nightshades such as tomatoes,
white potatoes, red potatoes, and peppers. In other words, eat like a
human being would have eaten prior to the agricultural revolution—
perhaps with the exception of all the modern, newfangled “Paleo-
approved” energy bars, drinks, and supplements that have saturated the
market! The best guide to more history and details of the Paleo diet is The
Paleo Solution by Robb Wolf.
The Paleo diet would be appropriate for someone sensitive to grains,
legumes, and dairy who wants to expand their eating beyond a more
restrictive protocol such as Autoimmune Paleo (AIP), and it may be
helpful for conditions of gut inflammation, autoimmune disease, or skin
--- END PAGE 1303 ---

--- PAGE 1304 ---
issues such as acne or eczema. Some research even suggests that type 2
diabetes may improve with a Paleo diet. This is because insulin resistance
may be caused by inflammation, and the Paleo diet eliminates common
inflammatory foods. It’s a good choice if you have any indicators of dairy
sensitivities, autoimmune disorders, or gut inflammation.
A note on dairy: You can consume dairy on a Paleo diet if you tolerate
it well and it comes from grass-fed cows, which produce milk that is
higher in anti-inflammatory omega-3 fatty acids and lower in inflammatory
omega-6s. Grain-fed cows absorb gut-irritating lectins from their feed that
are then concentrated in their milk, which can contribute to inflammation
in people who drink that milk. Ideally, any milk consumed on a Paleo diet
(or, in my opinion, any other diet) should be A2 milk, which has more A2
than A1 casein—A1 casein can produce significant gut inflammation in
many individuals. Casein concentrations vary among breeds of cows, with
some breeds—such as Guernsey and Jersey cows—having very little to no
A1 casein. You can find more details at A2Milk.com.

Advanced

Although any of the intermediate diets can be followed indefinitely, I

MEDITERRANEAN DIET (LOW-CARB VERSION)
The Mediterranean diet is a plant- and omega-3-rich diet that is prevalent
in many longevity hot spots and Blue Zones (although it is possible that
the diet’s positive health effects may also be caused by lifestyle factors
such as fasting, seasonal eating, social meals, high intake of tannin-rich
beverages and wild plants, and limited meat consumption). It is a dietary
pattern inspired by the traditional eating habits of countries bordering the
Mediterranean Sea and emphasizes whole, minimally processed foods
such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, olive oil, fish,
and poultry while limiting intake of processed red meat, refined sugars,
and unhealthy fats. The diet is rich in fiber, antioxidants, healthy fats, and
phytonutrients, which have been shown to reduce inflammation, improve
blood lipid levels, lower blood pressure, and support heart health.
A low-carb twist on the Mediterranean diet merges the well-known
beneficial health impacts of the Mediterranean diet with the positive
metabolic effects of stable blood sugar, elevated ketones, fat-burning
metabolism, and low intake of processed starches and carbohydrates.
After all, a traditional, healthy Mediterranean meal doesn’t include
unlimited breadsticks and endless salad bowls drenched in vegetable oil,
and instead incorporates a much wider variety of plants, herbs, spices,
--- END PAGE 1305 ---

--- PAGE 1306 ---
fatty fish, avocados, olive oil, fermented dairy, artisanal cheeses, and more
in a rainbow of colors. Based on a large amount of epidemiological
research, this approach can be particularly effective for managing
cardiovascular conditions, improving heart health, and managing
metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, along with overall health span
and lifespan.

ANCESTRAL DIET
There are a variety of ways to customize the Weston A. Price diet to your
specific ancestry—a concept explored in chapter 19. In the book The Jungle
Effect, Dr. Daphne Miller explains the dietary wisdom of traditional
cultures whose diets are specific to their genes and ancestry. In her
research for the book (you can listen to my podcast with her, linked to on
BoundlessBook.com/21), Miller traveled to locations around the world
that she identified as “cold spots”—the opposite of hot spots!—that had a
remarkably low incidence of diseases such as diabetes, heart disease,
depression, colon cancer, breast cancer, and prostate cancer. It turned out
that many of the traditional cultures in these areas ate whole-food,
Weston A. Price–like diets that were specific to their traditions, ancestry,
and local environment. Many cold-spot inhabitants who relocate and
switch to a modern Western diet develop the very diseases for which their
traditional environments are cold spots!
The following are examples of cold spots and foods frequently eaten in
their ancestral diets:• 
Copper Canyon, Mexico (diabetes cold spot): corn, beans, squash,
peppers, nopal cactus, onions, cilantro, tomatoes, jicama, nuts,
--- END PAGE 1307 ---

--- PAGE 1308 ---
avocados•

Crete (heart disease cold spot): olive oil, chickpeas, lentils, whole-
grain pasta, potatoes, Swiss chard, kale, arugula, fish, red wine, figs,
walnuts•

Iceland (depression cold spot): fish, walnuts, purslane, flaxseed oil,
barley, rye, black tea, beans, split peas, potatoes, organic dairy
products, omega-3-enriched eggs, wild game, cabbage, bilberries•

Cameroon, West Africa (colon cancer cold spot): millet, teff, collard
greens, mustard greens, spinach, okra, plantains, beans, nuts, fish, wild
poultry and game, onions, tomatoes, bananas, yogurt, kefir, fermented
vegetables•

Okinawa, Japan (breast and prostate cancers cold spot): tofu,
tempeh, miso, fish, cabbage, bok choy, broccoli, kale, cauliflower,
brown rice, green tea, sea vegetables, sweet potatoes, mushrooms,
tomatoes, watermelons, grapefruit
For more information, read Dr. Miller’s book. Two other very good
titles on ancestral eating are Dr. Michael Smith’s Returning to an Ancestral
Diet and Stephen Le’s 100 Million Years of Food. Follow this eating plan if
you’ve done DNA testing and/or know your genetics and family history,
and you want to try eating more like your ancestors, which for many can
be ideal for health, cognition, performance, fertility, and longevity.
My “Boundless Busy Day” Diet
When I have an especially busy day, have a hectic travel day, or simply
don’t seem to have enough hours in the day but still have cognitive and

•

THE BOUNDLESS SUPPLEMENT
PROGRAM
In an ideal world, you would be able to fully customize every supplement
you take to your unique physiology—especially based on the information
in chapter 16—rather than follow a cookie-cutter program. But I’ve
included suggestions for supplementation protocols that paint with a
relatively broad brush and cover most bases for beginner, intermediate,
and advanced goals.
--- END PAGE 1310 ---

--- PAGE 1311 ---
Beginner
This protocol is for you if you are on a budget, want the lowest-hanging
fruit to give you 80 percent of the results with 20 percent of the expense
and effort, or need the minimum effective dose of supplementation to
look, feel, and perform as good as possible each day. Include the following:
• A multivitamin-multimineral complex, such as the Thorne Multi
capsules or MaryRuth’s liquid
• A good fish oil, such as Kion Omega—1–2 g per day with a meal
• Creatine—5 g per day, taken with a meal or smoothie or another
beverage, split into two 2.5 g servings (one in the morning, one in the
evening). The brand is not important as long as there are no added
sweeteners or fillers, and basic creatine monohydrate is fine. Kion
Creatine is my recommended option.
• If you are traveling or unable to eat a wide range of plants, an organic
greens powder such as AG1 Greens, Organifi Greens, or PaleoValley
• If you have difficulty sleeping, a sleep stack of magnesium, CBD, a
relaxing cocktail like Kion Sleep or any adaptogenic herbal blend, and,
if traveling, melatonin
• If you have gut issues or are unable to eat a wide variety of fermented
foods, a good probiotic and digestive enzyme blend, such as Seed
Probiotic or Thorne Advanced Digestive Enzymes
Intermediate
This protocol is for you if you have a slightly higher budget and want to
add supplements that can further enhance performance, longevity, and
mental function without breaking the bank.
Follow the beginner protocol and add the following:
--- END PAGE 1311 ---

--- PAGE 1312 ---
• 10–20 g of essential amino acids (EAAs) per day—preferably pre- or
postworkout without a meal
• Exogenous ketones for fasted or longer workouts or busy days
• Prior to your largest meal or largest carb-containing meal of the day,
insulin-stabilizing foods or supplements like bitter melon extract
(Kion Lean is good), Ceylon cinnamon, apple cider vinegar, berberine,
rosemary, turmeric, ginger, fenugreek, Gymnema sylvestre, or cayenne
• On more cognitively demanding days, coffee or green tea blended with
adaptogenic compounds such as L-theanine, tulsi, reishi or astragalus,
or small amounts of nicotine
Advanced
This protocol is for you if you are willing to invest in better living through
science so you can live as long as possible and perform at a high level, and
you desire to incorporate a full-blown Boundless supplement protocol.
Follow the intermediate protocol and add the following:
• Qualia, Nootopia, TianChi, Wukiyo, microdosing, or any other
nootropic stack or adaptogenic herb blend, especially on more
cognitively demanding days (see chapter 5)
• Hydrogen-rich water (dissolve tablets in water, use a hydrogen bottle,
purchase canned hydrogen-rich water, or use a hydrogen water–
generating machine)
• Daily supplementation with a good longevity stack, including some of
the most important recommendations from chapter 19, such as
spermidine, urolithin-A, astaxanthin, curcumin, CoQ10, PQQ,
glutathione or NAC, pterostilbene, MitoQ, astragalus, C60,
nicotinamide riboside (NR), and peptides
--- END PAGE 1312 ---

--- PAGE 1313 ---
Obviously, you may have specific needs for other supplements. For
example, if you have a high risk of cardiovascular disease or are managing
arterial plaque, you can consider red yeast rice, nitric oxide, vitamin K,
extra vitamin D, geranylgeraniol (GG), and some form of vascular support,
such as Calroy Arterosil. If you have slow methylation genetics, you may
benefit from extra methylfolate or a desiccated liver extract. For thyroid
support, you may need added minerals like iodine and selenium, along
with sea vegetable extracts such as kelp and dulse. You get the idea. But
the lists above should give you a very good foundation for setting up your
own supplement protocol.

The ability to look, feel, and perform at the human body’s full capacity
isn’t the stuff of lore—it’s all completely attainable. You really can have

you’re equipped with the road map for exactly how to get there.
